newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai exports to grow marginally in '96-think tank.
newsitem.headline: Thai exports to grow marginally in '96-think tank.

text.p: A leading private Thai research group forecast on Friday that exports this year would grow at their slowest pace since 1984 if the current sluggish trend continues.
The Thai Farmers Research Centre (TFRC) said that exports would rise about 4.9 percent in 1996 if they increase an average 6.0 percent during August/December.
Thai exports grew a hefty 23.6 percent in 1995 over 1994.
Bank of Thailand data showed that exports grew only 3.8 percent during January-July this year compared to 26.2 percent in the same period of 1995.

The TFRC quoted commerce ministry figures as saying exports to the United States and Japan, Thailand's biggest markets, posted sharply lower growth of 1.0 percent and 2.8 percent, respectively, in the first seven months of the year.
Exports to the U.S. and Japan 4.8 percent and 21.5 percent growth in the same period last year.

"The export slowdown in 1996 is an urgent and priority issue that the authorities should closely monitor in the rest of this year, as the export sector is a key growth engine of the Thai economy and domestic investment," the centre said.
The Bank of Thailand late last month scaled down its 1996 export growth projection to 10.2 percent from an earlier 17.4 percent.
Referring to the weak performance in the first seven months, a central bank economist said on Thursday the bank would need time to determine if the 10.2 percent target was achievable.
Olarn Chaipravat, president of the Thai Bankers Association, forecast on Friday that 1996 exports would grow about 7.0 percent over the previous year.
Thai Farmers Research's projection of 4.9 percent growth would be the weakest performance for Thai exports since 1984, when Thailand devalued its currency to boost exports.
The Thai central bank has ruled out a baht devaluation to push exports after market rumours of such a move put pressure on the currency in late July and early August.
The bank has sporadically intervened to defend the baht.
The TFRC said apart from export performance, the government should also focus on maintaining Thailand's traditional service account surplus, which helped ease its current account deficit.
Central bank figures showed that the Thai service account surplus, derived mainly from tourism revenue, has plunged since April. It swung into a rare deficit in May.

Dhana Siam Finance and Securities said on Friday if exports failed to pick up in the rest of 1996, the Thai current account deficit may widen to 8.9 percent of gross domestic product this year. That would be an increase from 7.8 percent last projected by the central bank and 8.1 percent in 1995.
